meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Say anything you want. Just spell my name right'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Babe Ruth. The saying is P. T. Barnum's, documented in 1888; the Ruth version is a 1932 newspaper columnist's invention.

answer.label: Not Babe Ruth — actually P. T. Barnum
answer.sourceLine: The saying is Barnum’s: newspapers in August 1888 reported him telling a woman who said she was writing a critical book about him to “say anything you like about me, but spell my name right.” The tighter Babe Ruth wording — “Say anything you want. Just spell my name right” — first appears in a Tampa Morning Tribune column of 12 March 1932, per Quote Investigator ↗ — framed as an imagined Q&A, not a real interview.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: P. T. Barnum, replying to a woman who told him she was writing a critical book about him (that fuller account — “Barnum and the Blackmailer” — runs in The St Johnsbury Caledonian, 9 August 1888)
Tampa Morning Tribune, 12 March 1932 — Red Newton’s column
Character in a columnist’s imagined Q&A; no documented first-hand utterance

source.excerpt: say anything you like about me, but spell my name right — P. T. B-a-r-n-u-m, P. T. Barnum — and I’ll be pleased anyway
trail: August 1888 — The earliest strong match: U.S. newspapers including The Evening News of Franklin, Pennsylvania (8 August) and The St Johnsbury Caledonian of Vermont (9 August) report Barnum’s reply to a would-be critic, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1912 (claimed) — George M. Cohan’s famous variant is dated to 1912 by a 1973 biography, but QI notes it has seen no supporting evidence for that early date ↗.
1930–1931 — The saying is circulating in sports pages: a Hackensack, New Jersey column in November 1930 and boxer Max Schmeling in January 1931 both use versions, as documented by QI ↗.
March 1932 — Only now does Babe Ruth appear — in Red Newton’s Tampa Morning Tribune column, in an invented interview. The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Babe Ruth page ↗ entirely.
source.excerptNote: That is the 1888 Barnum report, the earliest strong match Quote Investigator located. The compressed Babe Ruth form — “Say anything you want. Just spell my name right” — appears 44 years later in the Tampa Morning Tribune of 12 March 1932, inside a humorous mock dispatch, with a variant from the same columnist on 18 March 1932: “Print anything about me you want to, just spell my name right.”

source.useLine: Treated as in copyright — the 1932 Tampa Morning Tribune wording’s renewal status is unconfirmed, and for a 1932 US newspaper copyright depended on a renewal that was often never filed. A short, credited quote is generally fine for talks, teaching and internal decks; for commercial or published reuse, check the renewal record first.
source.rightsNote: Two different documents are in play. The 1888 newspaper report of Barnum’s remark, excerpted above, was published well before 1931 and is public domain in the United States. The exact wording this page asks about, however, first appears in a 1932 newspaper column — after the 1931 line — so we treat that text conservatively as in-copyright, since we have not confirmed its renewal status. Short quotation for commentary and identification is a separate question from ownership.

author.name: P. T. Barnum
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Who was P. T. Barnum?
author.bio: Phineas Taylor Barnum (5 July 1810 – 7 April 1891) was an American showman, businessman and politician, remembered for his museum of curiosities, his talent for publicity, and for founding the circus that became Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey. He built a career on the premise that attention itself was the asset — which is exactly the logic of this line. He is also the magnet for sayings he did not coin: Wikipedia notes there is no evidence he originated “there’s a sucker born every minute.”

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely shared lines in show business, and almost everyone quotable has been handed it at some point. The claimants below are the recurring ones.

items.scope: the exact wording on this page
items.why: The earliest instance Quote Investigator located is Red Newton’s column in the Tampa Morning Tribune, 12 March 1932 ↗ — presented as a mock dispatch in Q&A form, not a recorded interview. The saying was already in print decades earlier.

items.scope: the “as long as you say something about me” variant
items.why: A 1973 John McCabe biography of Cohan dates his version to 1912, but Quote Investigator reports it has not seen supporting evidence for that early date ↗. Cohan is nonetheless the name most reference works attach to the line.

items.who: Mae West, W. C. Fields, Will Rogers, Mark Twain, Oscar Wilde
items.why: All are listed among the claimants in Quote/Counterquote’s survey of the saying ↗, alongside “several prominent politicians” — the standard signature of a floating quotation.

The heavyweight champion is quoted in January 1931 saying of his critics, “I do not care so long as they spell the name right and come to see me fight” ↗ — a genuine use, but forty-plus years after Barnum.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s verdict ↗: P. T. Barnum deserves credit for the saying on the strength of the 1888 citations; Ruth, Schmeling, West and the rest were later users of a line already in circulation.

context.heading: Why the line keeps changing owners
lead: Every version of this saying does the same job: it converts criticism into publicity. That is why it migrates so easily. A showman, a Broadway producer, a boxer, a movie star and a ballplayer can all deliver it and have it sound in character — which is precisely the condition under which quotations drift.

Quote Investigator’s citation trail shows the drift happening in real time: an 1888 Barnum anecdote, boxing promoter James J. Johnston in a 1915 Damon Runyon column, a 1930 New Jersey sports item, boxer Max Schmeling in 1931, and only then Babe Ruth in 1932 — each speaker inheriting a line already in circulation.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator dates the exact wording to Red Newton’s column in the Tampa Morning Tribune of 12 March 1932, presented in a mock dispatch (“Private operative L2 reports from St. Petersburg”) with question-and-answer formatting — a humorous framing rather than a transcribed interview. The same columnist ran a variant on 18 March 1932: “Print anything about me you want to, just spell my name right.”

So even the earliest Ruth appearance is a columnist’s construction. That does not prove Ruth never said something similar in conversation — only that no documented instance from his own mouth has been produced, and that the idea was already forty-odd years old when it reached him.
context.pull: The sentiment is Barnum’s. Ruth is just the most quotable person it was ever handed to.
